Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Premier Financial Group Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, ladies and gentlemen, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to review Premier Financial Group's results for the second quarter of 2024. With me this morning are John Hayes, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Reynolds, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Risk Officer; and David Patel, Chief Credit Officer.

Before we begin, let me remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a discussion of these factors.

I will now turn the call over to John Hayes.

John Hayes:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Premier Financial Group delivered strong performance in the second quarter, driven by our commitment to customer service and operational excellence.

Our key priorities for this year remain focused on growing our core businesses, investing in technology and innovation, managing risk effectively, optimizing our capital allocation, and enhancing our employee engagement.

Now, I'd like to provide some highlights on a few key areas. On cost of deposits, average rates rose to 2.85% amid accelerating betas and intensifying competition from fintechs and peers. Our outlook for loan growth points to mid-single digits, paired with stable credit quality across segments. The macroeconomic environment features resilient U.S. growth but cooling labor markets and CRE pressures, which we're navigating well. Credit quality metrics showed NPLs improving to 0.82%, with charge-offs and delinquencies trending favorably overall. Finally, fee income rose 12% year-over-year, powered by robust wealth management, steady investment banking, and surging cards performance.

I will now turn the call over to Michael Reynolds to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you, John, and good morning. Premier Financial Group reported net income of $520 million for the second quarter, or $1.42 per share. Our results reflect strong revenue growth, disciplined expense management, and a healthy credit environment.

Net interest income increased 8% due to loan growth and improved net interest margin. Non-interest income was up 12% year-over-year to $950 million. Key performance indicators include ROE of 12.5% and a CET1 ratio of 11.8%. We are confident in our ability to achieve our financial goals for the year.

Let me now turn to our deposit franchise, specifically the dynamics around cost of deposits, where we've seen some meaningful shifts amid the ongoing rate environment. As you know, deposits remain the bedrock of our low-cost funding model here at Premier Financial Group, funding over 85% of our $300 billion loan portfolio. But with the Fed funds rate holding steady at 5.25-5.50% through Q2, deposit betas have accelerated, pushing average costs higher.

First, on average rates: Our total deposit cost averaged 2.85% in Q2, up 28 basis points quarter-over-quarter and 115 basis points year-over-year. This reflects a deposit beta of approximately 45% on the cumulative 525 basis points of Fed hikes since March 2022—right in line with the peer median for superregionals, as reported in the latest FDIC call report data. Drilling into the mix: non-interest-bearing deposits held steady at 0.05%, comprising 28% of total deposits—a testament to our sticky commercial relationships, where we've grown DDA balances by 4% quarter-over-quarter through treasury management cross-sells. Interest-bearing transaction and savings accounts rose to 1.92%, up 35 basis points quarter-over-quarter, driven by our tiered pricing on premium savings products. Money market and consumer CDs saw the sharpest move, averaging 3.75%—up 42 basis points—with CDs now at 4.25% for 12-month terms, as customers chase yield amid inverted curves. Brokered and wholesale CDs, which make up just 3% of our book, ticked up to 4.80%, but we've deliberately capped growth here to protect margins.

This mix shift contributed to a 12 basis points compression in our net interest margin to 3.42%—in line with JPMorgan's 3.45% and ahead of Bank of America's 3.12%, per their recent prints—but we view it as transitory given our deposit growth trajectory.

Now, competitive pressures are intensifying, particularly from fintech disruptors and money center banks. Ally and SoFi continue to lead with headline rates north of 4.5% on high-yield savings, pulling in digital-native customers and forcing incumbents like us to respond. In our core Midwest franchise—where we hold a top-5 market share in Ohio and Indiana—competition from PNC and Fifth Third has been aggressive, with their MMDA rates averaging 50-75 basis points above ours in key MSAs. Nationally, we've seen deposit migration to alternatives like brokerage cash sweep programs at Schwab and Fidelity, which offer 5%+ sweeps with FDIC pass-through—siphoning roughly 2-3% of retail balances industry-wide, per S&P Global data.

Regionally, the story varies. In the Southeast, where we've expanded via our 2023 Florida de novo charters, costs are elevated at 3.15% due to hot money inflows chasing sunbelt growth—think retirees rolling out of CDs at 1% into our 4.20% 18-month specials. Conversely, our Northeast commercial book in New York and Boston remains a haven, with costs at 2.40% thanks to relationship pricing tied to C&I lending; we've beta-managed these down to 35% through reciprocal business incentives. Out West, California pressures from Wells Fargo and digital players have capped our retail deposit growth at 1.5% quarter-over-quarter, prompting a pivot to muni depositors.

Strategically, we're not just reacting—we're ahead of the curve with several initiatives to optimize beta and defend core deposits. We've rolled out a precision pricing engine in Q1 across our 450 branches and app, this AI-driven tool dynamically adjusts rates based on customer tenure, balance tiers, and ZIP-code competition. It's shaved 15 basis points off our retail beta year-to-date by offering loyalty bumps—for example, plus 25 basis points for autotransfer customers.

On the commercial side, targeting a 60/40 retail/commercial mix shift, we've launched Premier Treasury Plus, bundling Zelle for Business, wire fee waivers, and 3.10% tiered DDA rates for $10 million-plus relationships. This has grown commercial non-interest-bearing deposits 7% quarter-over-quarter, outpacing peers.

For digital acquisition, while growing digital deposits 22% year-over-year to $18 billion, we've implemented yield caps at 4.00% for new online savings to avoid unsustainable beta creep, supplemented by FHLB advance laddering at 4.90% for any gaps.

We've also enhanced our beta forecasting model with machine learning on FDIC peer data and Fed dot plots, improving our forward beta accuracy to within 5 basis points, allowing proactive re-pricing 30 days ahead of rate moves.

Looking forward, we expect Q3 deposit costs to rise another 10-15 basis points to 2.95-3.00%, assuming no Fed cuts, with betas stabilizing at 40-45% as rate fatigue sets in—echoing the 2019 playbook. Our $5.2 billion deposit inflow in Q2 gives us ample liquidity with LCR at 118%, and we're prioritizing organic growth over paid media to keep costs below the 3.50% peer average. This positions us for NIM expansion to 3.55%+ in 2025 as cuts materialize, while maintaining ROA above 1.20%.

Turning now to our outlook for loan growth and credit quality, which we see as foundational to delivering sustainable, risk-adjusted returns in this dynamic environment. I'll walk you through our expectations for the next 12 to 18 months, grounded in our base-case macroeconomic scenario of mid-3% U.S. GDP growth, gradual Fed rate cuts to 4.25-4.50% by year-end 2025, and moderating inflation around 2.5%. We've stress-tested this against downside risks like persistent CRE weakness or a sharper slowdown in Europe, but our positioning remains resilient.

On loan growth outlook, we're targeting mid-single-digit expansion with disciplined underwriting. We expect full-year 2025 loan growth of 5% to 6% on an average balance basis, accelerating from the 4.2% achieved earlier this year. This builds on our diversified portfolio—now $300 billion in total loans outstanding—and reflects selective deployment of our $45 billion liquidity buffer, with a focus on high-return, low-risk segments.

Breaking it down by line of business: Commercial & Industrial, we project 6-7% growth here, driven by middle-market renewals and new originations in tech-enabled sectors like renewables and SaaS. Our C&I book, at $120 billion, benefits from our proprietary PremierScore AI platform, which has improved approval rates by 15% while tightening risk parameters—average loan-to-value now at 65%, down from 72% pre-2023. We've seen strong pipeline momentum in the Southeast U.S., where manufacturing reshoring is boosting demand; commitments rose 12% quarter-over-quarter. Nationally, we're capitalizing on peers like JPMorgan and Wells Fargo dialing back exposure amid higher-for-longer rates.

Commercial Real Estate: more cautious at 2-3% growth on our $55 billion portfolio, emphasizing multifamily and industrial over office. Delinquency rates here stabilized at 1.2% in Q2, versus the industry average of 1.8% per MBA data. We're actively managing maturities—$8 billion rolling in H1 2025—with 85% refinance capacity at current spreads. Regionally, Sun Belt markets like Dallas-Fort Worth remain robust at sub-1% delinquencies, while we've de-risked Northeast office by 20% through non-accrual transfers. Our partnership with Blackstone's real estate debt funds has unlocked $2 billion in co-originations, blending our balance sheet with their expertise for 9-10% risk-adjusted yields.

Consumer and Residential: 7-8% growth anticipated, led by mortgages at $65 billion, up 5.5% year-over-year, and auto loans at $25 billion. Mortgage originations should benefit from 30-year fixed rates dipping to 6.2-6.5%, with refi activity picking up—our digital mortgage platform processed 40% more apps via API integrations with leading tech stacks. Auto growth accelerates on pent-up demand and EV financing incentives; delinquencies remain pristine at 0.4%. Cards and unsecured lending, at $20 billion, grow modestly at 4%, supported by our FlexPay BNPL product, now with 2 million active users embedded in our mobile app.

Regionally, U.S. operations drive 70% of growth, with 8% expansion in the Midwest from agribusiness lending amid favorable commodity prices. Internationally, our Asia-Pacific franchise—via Premier Singapore—targets 10% growth in SME lending on a $15 billion book, leveraging ASEAN trade recovery and RMB cross-border facilities. Europe remains flat at 1-2%, as we navigate ECB policy divergence and selective funding of green bonds.

Key enablers include our $500 million tech investment this year, rolling out machine learning for dynamic pricing—boosting NIM accretion by 10 basis points—and blockchain-based syndication with platforms like Syndigo, reducing close times by 30%. We're allocating 60% of new loans to investment-grade equivalents with PD under 1%, ensuring ROE expansion to 12-13%.

On credit quality outlook: stability with buffers for volatility. Credit quality remains a competitive moat, with Q2 net charge-offs at 45 basis points, well below our 65 basis points long-term average and peers like Bank of America at 62 basis points. We expect NCOs to trough at 40-45 basis points in 2025 before edging to 50 basis points in a softening economy, supported by our $4.2 billion allowance for credit losses covering 147% of criticized loans and 3.1 times projected NCOs.

Under CECL, our reserve rate stands at 1.45% of loans, up 5 basis points quarter-over-quarter, reflecting macroeconomic overlays for unemployment ticking to 4.5%. Delinquencies are stable: overall 1.1% versus 1.3% industry per FDIC, with C&I at 0.8%, CRE at 1.2%, and consumer at 0.9%. Early-stage buckets improved to 0.6%, aided by proactive collections via our GenAI chatbot, which resolved 25% more workouts autonomously.

Forward-looking, our base case assumes no material deterioration, with PD models forecasting 20 basis points compression in C&I from capex cycles. Downside scenario—10% GDP drawdown—sees NCOs peak at 120 basis points, but our ACL build of $250-350 million in 2025 provides a 200 basis points buffer. Strategic de-risking includes tightening overlays on variable-rate loans, now 40% of portfolio and hedged via swaps, and exiting $1.5 billion in energy exposure post-OPEC+ cuts.

Regionally, U.S. consumer strength persists—FICO scores averaging 740 in originations—but we're vigilant on California wildfires impacting $500 million in residential. In APAC, Vietnam SME delinquencies at 1.5% warrant scrutiny amid export slowdowns, offset by our 20% collateralization threshold.

Loan growth and credit quality are symbiotic: we're pursuing growth at scale by targeting 1.5-2.0% NIM expansion through mix shift away from low-yield deposits and fee income from loan syndications, up 15% year-over-year. Capital deployment prioritizes buybacks over dividends until CET1 hits 11.5%, with excess directed to high-conviction loans yielding 450 basis points over Treasuries.

Before moving on, a quick note on the macroeconomic outlook and its impact. We've built our strategy around resilience in volatile cycles, leveraging our diversified franchise across retail banking, commercial lending, wealth management, and capital markets. Our CET1 ratio stands at a rock-solid 11.8%, well above regulatory requirements under Basel IV, positioning us to navigate headwinds while capitalizing on tailwinds.

The IMF's latest World Economic Outlook projects global GDP growth at 3.1% for 2024, a slight downgrade driven by persistent geopolitical tensions—ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East—and softening demand in key export markets. Inflation has moderated to 5.8% globally, but core pressures linger in services and commodities.

In the U.S., our core market representing 65% of our loan book, growth is tracking at 2.4% annualized in Q2, per the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker. The Fed's pivot to easing—anticipated cuts bringing the funds rate to 4.50-4.75%—is relief after 525 basis points of hikes. However, the labor market is cooling, with unemployment at 4.2% and JOLTS openings falling 7% year-over-year to 8.1 million. Consumer spending held steady at plus 2.1% real terms, but credit card delinquencies have risen to 3.2%, impacting our unsecured lending.

This is pressuring NIM industry-wide, with median bank NIM compressing to 3.15% from 3.45% a year ago per KBW data. At Premier, our NIM expanded 12 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 3.42%, thanks to our asset-sensitive balance sheet: 68% of loans variable-rate, re-pricing faster than our deposit beta of 65%. Deposit growth remains robust at plus 4.2% year-over-year, outpacing the industry's 2.8%, fueled by high-yield savings at 4.1% APY—competitive with Ally and SoFi—while non-interest-bearing deposits stabilized at 28% of total funding.

Credit quality is a watchpoint: NPLs rose modestly to 1.12% from 0.98% quarter-over-quarter, concentrated in CRE, where office exposure drags. Nationally, CRE vacancy rates hit 19.5% in Q2 per Moody's. Our CRE book is 8% of total loans at $28 billion, with office under 2%, stress-tested to 40% value decline under CCAR, maintaining coverage above 250%. We're managing via extensions on 15% of maturities and our AI-powered early-warning system, flagging 92% of potential downgrades 90 days ahead using 500+ data points.

In Europe, our EMEA operations, 12% of revenue, face stagnation: ECB forecasts 0.8% GDP growth. Rate cuts to 3.50% support mortgage refinancing—our UK buy-to-let up 6%—but energy costs cap upside. We've hedged 85% of Euro assets via swaps, limiting FX volatility.

In Asia-Pacific, 10% of revenue via our Singapore hub, China's property woes push shadow banking NPLs to 1.9% per PBOC. Our exposure is $4.2 billion, focused on tech and renewables, with loan growth plus 3.1% year-over-year. India's 6.8% GDP drives plus 12% in SME lending with partners.

Strategically, we're accelerating digital transformation: our mobile app has 18 million active users, up 22% year-over-year, with embedded finance boosting fee income 14% to $1.2 billion. We've invested $250 million in gen-AI for risk management, partnering to reduce loss rates 18% in consumer lending.

Diversification into fees: wealth AUM $450 billion, plus 9% quarter-over-quarter. ESG products grew 25% to $15 billion.

Capital: $12 billion excess, returning 60% via $3 billion buybacks, 20% complete, and dividend hike to $0.62 per share.

For 2025, U.S. GDP 1.8-2.2%, Fed to 3.75%, supporting mid-single-digit loan growth, NIM 3.4-3.5%, ROTE to 13%. Risks like harder landing mitigated by LCR 135%.

Now, turning to credit quality metrics in more detail, which continue to reflect the strength of our diversified $300 billion loan portfolio. We've maintained disciplined underwriting and proactive management in this rate environment, with ALLL at 1.28% of loans—up 5 basis points sequentially, provisioned at 155% coverage of NPLs.

Headline numbers: NPL ratio improved to 0.82% from 0.89% prior quarter and 1.05% year-ago, driven by paydowns in CRE and consumer installment. Delinquencies 30 days or more ticked up modestly to 2.15% from 2.08%—below FDIC industry 2.45%—stable year-over-year. NCOs at 0.42% annualized, up slightly from 0.38% but down from 0.55% last year.

By segment, consumer banking, 45% of loans, saw credit card delinquencies to 3.25% from 3.12%, in line with peers, as revolving balances rise amid high APRs. Vintage analysis shows recent originations 15-20 basis points better, with FICO at 725 average and Plaid integrations.

Auto lending, 12% of book, NPLs steady at 0.95%, charge-offs to 0.68% on repo costs; AutoEdge telematics reduces early delinquencies 25%.

Residential mortgages, 25%, NPLs 0.65%—half national average—delinquencies flat at 1.40%, 85% fixed-rate.

Commercial, 38%, NPLs 0.75%, down 10 basis points; office classified to 2.1% in stressed markets, but resolved $250 million criticized via restructurings.

Geographically, Southeast/Texas NPLs 0.65% on inflows; Northeast commercial 1.15%; Europe pristine at 0.45%.

Technical enhancements: EWS 2.0 improves prediction to 88%, intervening 45 days early, shaving 8 basis points off delinquencies. DFAST confirms adequacy; CECL overlays added $75 million provision.

Strategically, exiting subprime auto, growing prime personal loans up 12% year-over-year at 0.40% NPLs, expanding Sun Belt CRE. Guidance: NPLs 0.80-0.90%, NCOs 0.40-0.50%, delinquencies flat absent recession.

Finally, on fee income breakdown, which totaled $2.8 billion for the quarter, up 12% year-over-year and 5% quarter-over-quarter. This resilience across wealth management, investment banking, and cards underscores diversification despite macro challenges. Core fees grew 9% excluding prior reserve reversal, from 8% client asset expansion, 15% card volumes, and advisory wins.

Wealth management: $1.4 billion, plus 14% year-over-year. AUM record $2.1 trillion on 11% appreciation, S&P 18% YTD, $28 billion inflows. HNWI $18 billion new; ESG to $450 billion; Americas 60% growth, APAC star at 22%. AI robo-advisory boosts margins 50 basis points; BlackRock partnership targets 15-20% AUM growth.

Investment banking: $850 million, plus 2% year-over-year. Advisory up 18% to $420 million on $450 billion M&A volume, #4 rank; ECM/DCM down on IPO drought. U.S./APAC 40% each; fintech/renewables focus, blockchain cuts execution 30%. Expect 10-15% growth H1 2025.

Cards: $550 million, plus 22% year-over-year. Volumes $280 billion, plus 14%; interchange $360 million up 25% on premium Visa; co-brands add accounts. Delinquencies 2.8%, NCOs 3.1% below average. U.S. 85%, APAC 30%; contactless 85%, BNPL lifts tickets 15%.

Fee growth validates One Bank strategy, margins to 42%. Q3 guide 10-13%.

Lisa Chen:
Thank you, Michael. As Chief Risk Officer, I would like to briefly discuss our risk management framework. We continue to prioritize proactive risk identification and mitigation. Our key focus areas include credit risk in CRE and consumer segments, and operational risks from cyber threats and third-party vendors. We remain vigilant in monitoring emerging risks like geopolitical tensions and adapting our strategies accordingly.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator:
Ladies and gentlemen, if you'd like to ask a question, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star then two. [Pause] Our first question comes from Mike Sullivan with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Mike Sullivan:
Good morning. Can you provide more detail on cost of deposits average rates and competitive pressures?

John Hayes:
Thanks, Mike. As Michael outlined comprehensively, our total deposit cost hit 2.85% with betas at 45%, in line with peers, but we've managed the mix well—non-interest-bearing steady at 28%—and our precision pricing and commercial optimization initiatives are keeping us ahead. Competition from fintechs is real, but our regional franchises and loyalty programs are stabilizing inflows. We're confident in further beta stabilization.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Jennifer Patel with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.

Jennifer Patel:
What are your expectations for loan growth and credit quality?

Michael Reynolds:
Great question, Jennifer. To reiterate, we're guiding 5-6% loan growth in 2025, led by C&I at 6-7% and consumer at 7-8%, with CRE cautious at 2-3%. Credit quality stays strong—NCOs 40-45 bps trough—with ACL buffers and AI tools providing resilience even in downside scenarios. Our diversified book and tech investments support risk-adjusted returns outperforming peers.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Robert Chen with Citigroup. Please go ahead.

Robert Chen:
Can you comment on the credit quality of the CRE portfolio?

David Patel:
Absolutely, Robert. Our CRE book at $55 billion, or about 18% of loans, shows delinquencies stable at 1.2%, well below industry 1.8%. Office is limited and de-risked, with Sun Belt multifamily strong. We've managed maturities proactively, Blackstone partnerships add yield, and our early-warning systems keep classifieds contained—coverage robust at over 250% in stress.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn the conference back over to John Hayes for any closing remarks.

John Hayes:
Thank you for your interest in Premier Financial Group. We appreciate you joining us today. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.

Intense competition from fintechs (Ally/SoFi >4.5%), peers, and brokerage sweeps; countered by precision pricing AI, commercial bundling, yield caps, expecting Q3 rise to 2.95-3.00% with stabilizing betas.

Credit quality stable with NCOs at 40-45 bps (below 65 bps long-term avg), NPLs 0.80-0.90%, delinquencies flat, supported by $4.2B ACL (1.45% of loans) and AI risk tools even in downside scenarios.

Resilient growth but cooling labor (unemployment 4.2%), CRE/office pressures (vacancy 19.5%), NIM compression; Premier resilient via asset-sensitive balance sheet (NIM 3.42%), diversified ops, LCR 118-135%, positioning for ROE 12-13%.

Trends favorable overall (improved early buckets), segment-stable (CRE 1.2%, consumer cards 3.25%), aided by AI EWS, ACL 1.28-1.45%; de-risking in office/energy.
